claim: The Alk receptor tyrosine kinase is expressed in the visceral mesoderm, central nervous system (CNS), and at neuromuscular junctions (NMJ) in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, Alk is expressed in the visceral mesoderm, central nervous system (CNS), and at neuromuscular junctions (NMJ).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the expression pattern of Alk in Drosophila.

claim: The critical role of Drosophila Alk and its ligand Jelly belly (Jeb) in the development of the embryonic visceral mesoderm has been extensively studied.
source: The critical role of Drosophila Alk and its ligand Jelly belly (Jeb) in the development of the embryonic visceral mesoderm has been extensively studied (Englund et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2003; Lorén et al., 2003; Mendoza-Garcia et al., 2021; Mendoza-García et al., 2017; Pfeifer et al., 2022; Popichenko et al., 2013; Reim et al., 2012; Schaub and Frasch, 2013; Shirinian et al., 2007; Stute et al., 2004; Varshney and Palmer, 2006; Wolfstetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: Alk signaling has been implicated in targeting of photoreceptor axons in the developing optic lobes.
source: In the CNS, Alk signaling has been implicated in diverse functions, including targeting of photoreceptor axons in the developing optic lobes (Bazigou et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bazigou et al., 2007.

claim: Alk signaling has been implicated in regulation of NMJ synaptogenesis and architecture.
source: In the CNS, Alk signaling has been implicated in diverse functions, including targeting of photoreceptor axons in the developing optic lobes (Bazigou et al., 2007), regulation of NMJ synaptogenesis and architecture (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2010; Rohrbough et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rohrbough and Broadie, 2010 and Rohrbough et al., 2013.

claim: Alk signaling has been implicated in mushroom body neuronal differentiation.
source: In the CNS, Alk signaling has been implicated in diverse functions, including targeting of photoreceptor axons in the developing optic lobes (Bazigou et al., 2007), regulation of NMJ synaptogenesis and architecture (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2010; Rohrbough et al., 2013), and mushroom body neuronal differentiation (Pfeifer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pfeifer et al., 2022.

claim: Roles for Alk in neuronal regulation of growth and metabolism, organ sparing and proliferation of neuroblast clones, as well as sleep and long-term memory formation in the CNS have been reported.
source: In addition, roles for Alk in neuronal regulation of growth and metabolism, organ sparing and proliferation of neuroblast clones, as well as sleep and long-term memory formation in the CNS have been reported (Bai and Sehgal, 2015; Cheng et al., 2011; Gouzi et al., 2011; Orthofer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bai and Sehgal, 2015; Cheng et al., 2011; Gouzi et al., 2011; Orthofer et al., 2020.

claim: The protein tyrosine phosphatase Corkscrew is a molecular component of Drosophila Alk signaling in the larval CNS.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying these Alk-driven phenotypes are currently under investigation, with some molecular components of Drosophila Alk signaling in the larval CNS, such as the protein tyrosine phosphatase Corkscrew, identified in recent BioID-based in vivo proximity labeling analyses (Uçkun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uçkun et al., 2021.

claim: Targeted DamID (TaDa) employs a prokaryotic DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam) to specifically methylate adenines within GATC sequences present in the genome, creating unique GAmeTC marks.
source: TaDa employs a prokaryotic DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam) to specifically methylate adenines within GATC sequences present in the genome, creating unique GAmeTC marks.
evidence: This is a direct description of the TaDa methodology.

claim: In TaDa, expression of Dam fused to Pol II results in GAmeTC marks on sequences adjacent to the Pol II binding site and can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system to achieve cell type-specific transcriptional profiling.
source: In TaDa, expression of Dam fused to Pol II results in GAmeTC marks on sequences adjacent to the Pol II binding site and can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system to achieve cell type-specific transcriptional profiling (Southall et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Southall et al., 2013.

claim: Tissue-specific TaDa analysis of Alk signaling has previously been used to identify Alk transcriptional targets in the embryonic visceral mesoderm, such as the transcriptional regulator Kahuli.
source: Tissue-specific TaDa analysis of Alk signaling, while genetically manipulating Alk signaling output, has previously been used to identify Alk transcriptional targets in the embryonic visceral mesoderm, such as the transcriptional regulator Kahuli (Mendoza-Garcia et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendoza-Garcia et al., 2021.

claim: TaDa identified 2502 loci with decreased Pol II occupancy (logFC≥2, FDR≤0.05) when comparing AlkDN to control samples in the Drosophila larval CNS.
source: To further analyze transcriptional targets of Alk signaling, we focused on loci exhibiting decreased Pol II occupancy when compared with controls, identifying 2502 loci with logFC≥2, FDR≤0.05 (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data presented in Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Genes previously known to be associated with Alk signaling, such as kirre, RhoGAP15B, C3G, mib2, and mamo, were identified among downregulated loci in the TaDa analysis.
source: Genes previously known to be associated with Alk signaling, such as kirre, RhoGAP15B, C3G, mib2, and mamo, were identified among downregulated loci (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1d showing these genes highlighted in the volcano plot.

claim: 775 common genes were identified when comparing CNS TaDa Alk targets with previously published embryonic visceral mesoderm TaDa datasets.
source: We compared CNS TaDa Alk targets with our previously published embryonic visceral mesoderm TaDa datasets that were derived under similar experimental conditions (Mendoza-Garcia et al., 2021) and found 775 common genes (Figure 1e, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1e showing a Venn diagram of the overlap.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of TaDa downregulated genes identified GO terms in agreement with previously reported Alk functions in the CNS such as axon guidance, determination of adult lifespan, nervous system development, regulation of gene expression, mushroom body development, behavioral response to ethanol and locomotor rhythm.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis identified GO terms in agreement with previously reported Alk functions in the CNS (Bai and Sehgal, 2015; Bazigou et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2011; Gouzi et al., 2011; Orthofer et al., 2020; Pfeifer et al., 2022; Rohrbough and Broadie, 2010; Rohrbough et al., 2013; Woodling et al., 2020) such as axon guidance, determination of adult lifespan, nervous system development, regulation of gene expression, mushroom body development, behavioral response to ethanol and locomotor rhythm (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 1f showing GO term enrichment, and references previous studies.

claim: AUCell enrichment analysis of the top 500 TaDa hits identified 786 cells (out of 3598) in the third instar larval CNS scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Enrichment of TaDa loci were identified by using AUCell, an area-under-the-curve-based enrichment score method, employing the top 500 TaDa hits (Aibar et al., 2017; Figure 2a and b, Supplementary file 1). This analysis identified 786 cells (out of 3598), mainly located in a distinct cluster of mature neurons that robustly express both Alk and jeb (Figure 2b, red circle; Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2b showing the AUCell enrichment analysis.

claim: The cluster of cells enriched for TaDa loci was defined as neuroendocrine cells based on canonical markers, such as the neuropeptides Lk (Leucokinin), Nplp1 (Neuropeptide-like precursor 1), Dh44 (Diuretic hormone 44), Dh31 (Diuretic hormone 31), sNPF (short neuropeptide F), AstA (Allatostatin A), and the enzyme Pal2 (Peptidyl-α-hydroxyglycine-α-amidating lyase 2) as well as Eip74EF (Ecdysone-induced protein 74EF), and Rdl (resistance to dieldrin).
source: This cluster was defined as neuroendocrine cells based on canonical markers, such as the neuropeptides Lk (Leucokinin), Nplp1 (Neuropeptide-like precursor 1), Dh44 (Diuretic hormone 44), Dh31 (Diuretic hormone 31), sNPF (short neuropeptide F), AstA (Allatostatin A), and the enzyme Pal2 (Peptidyl-α-hydroxyglycine-α-amidating lyase 2) as well as Eip74EF (Ecdysone-induced protein 74EF), and Rdl (resistance to dieldrin) (Guo et al., 2019; Hückesfeld et al., 2021; Takeda and Suzuki, 2022; Torii, 2009; Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figures 2d-f showing marker expression, and references previous studies.

claim: Alk protein is expressed in a subset of neuroendocrine cells in the larval central brain, ventral nerve cord, and neuroendocrine corpora cardiaca cells.
source: To further explore the observed enrichment of Alk-regulated TaDa loci in neuroendocrine cells, we used a Dimm transcription factor reporter (Dimm-Gal4>UAS-GFPcaax), as a neuroendocrine marker (Park et al., 2008), to confirm Alk protein expression in a subset of neuroendocrine cells in the larval central brain, ventral nerve cord, and neuroendocrine corpora cardiaca cells (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing immunostaining.

claim: CG4577 was the only candidate which met the stringent criteria of being upregulated in Alk gain-of-function conditions, downregulated in Alk loss-of-function conditions, and expressed in Alk-positive cells in the scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Notably, the only candidate which met these stringent criteria was CG4577, which encodes an uncharacterized putative neuropeptide precursor (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3b showing a Venn diagram.

claim: CG4577 exhibited decreased Pol II occupancy in AlkDN samples.
source: CG4577 exhibited decreased Pol II occupancy in AlkDN samples (Figure 3c)
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3c showing TaDa Pol II occupancy.

claim: CG4577 transcripts were upregulated in AlkY1355S gain-of-function conditions and downregulated in AlkΔRA loss-of-function conditions.
source: CG4577 transcripts were upregulated in AlkY1355S gain-of-function conditions and downregulated in AlkΔRA loss-of-function conditions (Figure 3d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3d showing expression levels.

claim: Expression of CG4577 was almost exclusively restricted to neuroendocrine cell clusters in the scRNA-seq dataset.
source: In agreement with a potential role as a neuropeptide precursor, expression of CG4577 was almost exclusively restricted to neuroendocrine cell clusters in our scRNA-seq dataset (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3e showing UMAP plots.

claim: CG4577-RA encodes a 445 amino acid prepropeptide with a 27 amino acid N-terminal signal peptide sequence as predicted by SignalP-5.0.
source: CG4577-RA encodes a 445 amino acid prepropeptide with a 27 amino acid N-terminal signal peptide sequence as predicted by SignalP-5.0 (Figure 3f; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 3f showing the amino acid sequence, and references SignalP-5.0 prediction.

claim: Analysis of CG4577-PA at the amino acid level identified a high percentage of glutamine residues (43 of 445; 9%), including six tandem glutamine repeats.
source: Analysis of CG4577-PA at the amino acid level identified a high percentage of glutamine residues (43 of 445; 9%), including six tandem glutamine repeats (amino acids 48–56, 59–62, 64–71, 116–118, 120–122, and 148–150) of unknown function as well as a lack of cysteine residues.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text based on amino acid sequence analysis.

claim: The CG4577 preproprotein has an acidic pI of 5.1 and carries a net negative charge of 6.
source: The preproprotein has an acidic pI of 5.1 and carries a net negative charge of 6.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text based on protein property analysis.

claim: Several poly- and dibasic proprotein convertase (PC) cleavage sites were predicted in the CG4577 preproprotein.
source: Several poly- and dibasic proprotein convertase (PC) (proprotein convertase) cleavage sites were also predicted (KR, KK, RR, RK) (Pauls et al., 2014; Southey et al., 2006; Veenstra, 2000; Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 3f, and references previous studies on PC cleavage site prediction.

claim: The CG4577 propeptide does not contain cysteine residues and is unable to form intracellular or dimeric disulfide bridges.
source: Since the propeptide does not contain cysteine residues, it is unable to form intracellular or dimeric disulfide bridges.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text based on amino acid sequence analysis.

claim: A second transcript, CG4577-RB, encodes a 446 amino acid protein with only two amino acid changes compared to CG4577-RA.
source: A second transcript, CG4577-RB, encodes a 446 amino acid protein with only two amino acid changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1c showing the alignment.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of CG4577 relative to known Drosophila neuropeptide precursors failed to identify strong homology.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of CG4577 relative to known Drosophila neuropeptide precursors failed to identify strong homology in keeping with the known low sequence conservation of neuropeptide prepropeptides outside their bioactive peptide stretches.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: CG4577 orthologs were obtained across the Drosophilids, Brachyceran flies, and Dipterans, but no orthologs were found at higher taxonomic levels.
source: Next, we searched for CG4577 orthologs across Metazoa. We obtained orthologs across the Drosophilids, Brachyceran flies, and Dipterans. No orthologs were found at higher taxonomic levels, suggesting that CG4577 either originated in Dipterans or has a high sequence variability at higher taxonomic levels.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text based on ortholog search results.

claim: Alignment of the predicted amino acid sequences of the Dipteran CG4577 orthologs revealed several conserved peptide stretches framed by canonical PC cleavage sites that might represent bioactive peptide sequences.
source: To identify conserved peptide stretches indicating putative bioactive peptide sequences, we aligned the predicted amino acid sequences of the Dipteran CG4577 orthologs. This revealed several conserved peptide stretches (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) framed by canonical PC cleavage sites that might represent bioactive peptide sequences.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing the alignment.

claim: CG4577 protein is expressed in a 'sparkly' pattern in neurons of the third instar central brain as well as in distinct cell bodies and neuronal processes in the ventral nerve cord.
source: CG4577 protein was expressed in a 'sparkly' pattern in neurons of the third instar central brain as well as in distinct cell bodies and neuronal processes in the ventral nerve cord, prompting us to name CG4577 as Sparkly (Spar) (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4a and 4b showing immunostaining.

claim: Co-labeling of Spar and Alk confirmed the expression of Spar in a subset of Alk-expressing cells.
source: Co-labeling of Spar and Alk confirmed the expression of Spar in a subset of Alk-expressing cells, in agreement with our transcriptomics analyses (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing co-labeling.

claim: Spar is expressed in neuronal processes which emerge from the ventral nerve cord and appear to innervate larval body wall muscle number 8.
source: In addition, we also observed expression of Spar in neuronal processes which emerge from the ventral nerve cord and appear to innervate larval body wall muscle number 8, that may be either Leukokinin (Lk) or cystine-knot glycoprotein hormone GPB5 expressing neurons (Figure 4b; Cantera and Nässel, 1992; Sellami et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 4b showing immunostaining, and references previous studies.

claim: Spar antibody specificity was confirmed in C155-Gal4>UAS-Spar-RNAi larvae, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of Spar resulted in loss of detectable signal.
source: Spar antibody specificity was confirmed in both C155-Gal4>UAS-Spar-RNAi larvae, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of Spar resulted in loss of detectable signal (Figure 4c–c')
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4c-c' showing reduced Spar signal.

claim: Spar antibody specificity was confirmed in C155-Gal4>UAS Spar larvae, exhibiting ectopic Spar expression in the larval CNS and photoreceptors of the eye disc.
source: Spar antibody specificity was confirmed in both C155-Gal4>UAS-Spar-RNAi larvae, where RNAi-mediated knockdown of Spar resulted in loss of detectable signal (Figure 4c–c'), and in C155-Gal4>UAS Spar larvae, exhibiting ectopic Spar expression in the larval CNS and photoreceptors of the eye disc (Figure 4d–d').
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4d-d' showing increased Spar signal.

claim: Co-labeling with antibodies against Dimm confirmed the expression of Spar in Dimm-positive peptidergic neuroendocrine cells in the larval CNS.
source: To further address Spar expression in the neuroendocrine system, we co-labeled with antibodies against Dimm to identify peptidergic neuronal somata (Allan et al., 2005) in a Dimm-Gal4>UAS-GFPcaax background. This further confirmed the expression of Spar in Dimm-positive peptidergic neuroendocrine cells in the larval CNS (Figure 4e–e'', Figure 4—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4e-e'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Co-staining of Spar and Dimm in the adult CNS showed similar results to the larval CNS.
source: Moreover, co-staining of Spar and Dimm in the adult CNS showed similar results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing co-staining.

claim: A significant increase in Spar protein was observed in AlkY1355S CNS.
source: We observed a significant increase in Spar protein in AlkY1355S CNS, while levels of Spar in AlkΔRA CNS were not significantly altered (Figure 4f–h, quantified in i).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4f-i showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Levels of Spar in AlkΔRA CNS were not significantly altered compared to controls.
source: We observed a significant increase in Spar protein in AlkY1355S CNS, while levels of Spar in AlkΔRA CNS were not significantly altered (Figure 4f–h, quantified in i).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4f-i showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Overexpression of Jeb (C155-Gal4>jeb) significantly increased Spar levels when compared with controls (C155-Gal4>UAS-GFPcaax).
source: In agreement, overexpression of Jeb (C155-Gal4>jeb) significantly increased Spar levels when compared with controls (C155-Gal4>UAS-GFPcaax) (Figure 4j–l, quantified in m).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4j-m showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Overexpression of dominant-negative Alk (C155-Gal4>UAS-AlkDN) did not result in significantly decreased Spar levels.
source: Again, overexpression of dominant-negative Alk (C155-Gal4>UAS-AlkDN) did not result in significantly decreased Spar levels (Figure 4l, quantified in m).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 4l and 4m showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Activation of Alk signaling increases Spar protein levels.
source: Thus activation of Alk signaling increases Spar protein levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased Spar levels upon Alk activation.

claim: While bulk RNA-seq and TaDa datasets show a reduction in Spar transcript levels in Alk loss-of-function conditions, this reduction is not reflected at the protein level.
source: However, while our bulk RNA-seq and TaDa datasets show a reduction in Spar transcript levels in Alk loss-of-function conditions, this reduction is not reflected at the protein level.
evidence: This is a statement comparing transcript and protein level data.

claim: Spar expression is responsive to Alk signaling in CNS, although Alk is not critically required to maintain Spar protein levels.
source: Taken together, these observations confirm that Spar expression is responsive to Alk signaling in CNS, although Alk is not critically required to maintain Spar protein levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: LC-MS peptidomic analysis of brain extracts from 5-day-old male control flies identified several peptides derived from the Spar propeptide by mass matching in non-digested extracts.
source: To provide biochemical evidence for the expression of Spar, we re-analyzed data from a previous LC-MS peptidomic analysis of brain extracts from 5-day-old male control flies and flies deficient for carboxypeptidase D (dCPD, SILVER) (Pauls et al., 2019), an enzyme that removes the basic C-terminal amino acid of peptides originating from PC cleavage of the proprotein. This analysis identified several peptides derived from the Spar propeptide by mass matching in non-digested extracts from genetic control brains (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 5 showing identified peptides, and references a previous study.

claim: One peptide (SEEASAVPTAD) derived from the Spar propeptide was obtained by de novo sequencing.
source: These included peptides that are framed by dibasic prohormone cleavage sequences in the propeptide, one of which (SEEASAVPTAD) was also obtained by de novo sequencing (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5 showing the identified peptide.

claim: The Spar precursor is expressed and is processed into multiple peptides by PCs and possibly also other proteases.
source: This result demonstrates that the Spar precursor is expressed and is processed into multiple peptides by PCs and possibly also other proteases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Analysis of the brain of svr mutant flies yielded peptides C-terminally extended by the dibasic cleavage sequence (SEEASAVPTADKK, FNDMRLKR), thereby confirming canonical PC processing of the Spar propeptide.
source: Analysis of the brain of svr mutant flies yielded similar results, but further revealed peptides C-terminally extended by the dibasic cleavage sequence (SEEASAVPTADKK, FNDMRLKR) (Figure 5), thereby confirming canonical PC processing of the Spar propeptide.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5 showing the identified peptides.

claim: The phylogenetically most conserved peptide sequence of the Spar precursor (DTQLNPADMLALVALVEAGERA) framed by dibasic cleavage sites was among the identified peptides yet occurred only in control but not svr mutant brains.
source: Of note, the phylogenetically most conserved peptide sequence of the Spar precursor (DTQLNPADMLALVALVEAGERA, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) framed by dibasic cleavage sites was among the identified peptides yet occurred only in control but not svr mutant brains (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5 showing the identified peptides.

claim: Spar is expressed in a subset of PDF-positive ventral lateral neuron (LNv) clock neurons.
source: These included the PDF-positive ventral lateral neuron (LNv) clock neurons (Figure 6a–b'')
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6a-b'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Spar is expressed in a subset of Dh44-positive neurons.
source: These included the PDF-positive ventral lateral neuron (LNv) clock neurons (Figure 6a–b''), Dh44-positive neurons (Figure 6c–d'')
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6c-d'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Spar is expressed in a subset of Ilp2 neurons in the central brain.
source: These included the PDF-positive ventral lateral neuron (LNv) clock neurons (Figure 6a–b''), Dh44-positive neurons (Figure 6c–d''), a subset of Ilp2 neurons in the central brain (Figure 6e–f'')
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6e-f'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Spar is expressed in several AstA-positive neurons in the central brain and ventral nerve cord.
source: These included the PDF-positive ventral lateral neuron (LNv) clock neurons (Figure 6a–b''), Dh44-positive neurons (Figure 6c–d''), a subset of Ilp2 neurons in the central brain (Figure 6e–f'') and several AstA-positive neurons in the central brain and ventral nerve cord (Figure 6g–h'').
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 6g-h'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Spar is co-expressed in some Lk-positive neurons in the central brain and ventral nerve cord, that include the neuronal processes converging on body wall muscle 8.
source: We also noted co-expression in some Lk-positive neurons in the central brain and ventral nerve cord, that include the neuronal processes converging on body wall muscle 8 (Figure 6i–l''; Cantera and Nässel, 1992).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figures 6i-l'' showing co-labeling, and references a previous study.

claim: Similar Spar co-expression with PDF, Dh44, Ilp2, and AstA was observed in adult CNS.
source: Similar Spar co-expression with PDF, Dh44, Ilp2, and AstA was observed in adult CNS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing co-labeling.

claim: Overexpression of Spar (C155-Gal4>Spar) or Spar RNAi (C155-Gal4>Spar RNAi) in CNS does not significantly affect pupal size compared to controls.
source: Since previous reports have shown that Jeb overexpression in the larval CNS results in a small pupal size (Gouzi et al., 2011), we measured pupal size on ectopic expression of Spar (C155-Gal4>Spar) and Spar RNAi (C155-Gal4>Spar RNAi), noting no significant difference compared to controls (C155-Gal4>+ and C155-Gal4>jeb) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing pupal size measurements.

claim: A Spar loss-of-function allele (SparΔExon1) was generated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated non-homologous end-joining, resulting in the deletion of a 716 bp region including the Spar TSS and exon 1.
source: To further investigate the function of Spar, we generated a Spar loss-of-function allele by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated non-homologous end-joining, resulting in the deletion of a 716 bp region including the Spar TSS and exon 1 (hereafter referred as SparΔExon1) (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7a showing the gene locus and deletion.

claim: Immunoblotting analysis indicated a 35 kDa protein present in the wild-type (w1118) controls that was absent in SparΔExon1 mutant CNS lysates.
source: Immunoblotting analysis indicated a 35 kDa protein present in the wild-type (w1118) controls that was absent in SparΔExon1 mutant CNS lysates (Figure 7b; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 7b showing the immunoblot.

claim: SparΔExon1 shows a complete abrogation of larval and adult Spar expression.
source: SparΔExon1 shows a complete abrogation of larval and adult Spar expression, consistent with the reduction observed when Spar RNAi was employed (Figure 7c–d').
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 7c-d' showing immunostaining.

claim: SparΔExon1 flies were viable, and no gross morphological phenotypes were observed.
source: SparΔExon1 flies were viable, and no gross morphological phenotypes were observed, similar to loss of function mutants in several previously characterized neuropeptides such as PDF, drosulfakinin, and neuropeptide F (Liu et al., 2019; Renn et al., 1999; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and references previous studies on neuropeptide mutants.

claim: Spar is expressed in ventral lateral neuron (LNv), dorsal lateral neuron (LNd), and dorsal neuron 1 (DN1) circadian neuronal populations, employing publicly available RNA-seq data.
source: A previous report noted expression of Spar in the LNv, dorsal lateral neuron (LNd), and dorsal neuron 1 (DN1) populations of adult Drosophila circadian clock neurons (Abruzzi et al., 2017; Figure 7e, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 7e showing expression data, and references a previous study.

claim: A meta-analysis of the publicly available single-cell transcriptomics of circadian clock neurons indicated that almost all adult clusters of clock neurons express Spar.
source: A meta-analysis of the publicly available single-cell transcriptomics of circadian clock neurons indicated that almost all adult clusters of clock neurons express Spar (Ma et al., 2021; Figure 7f).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text, supported by Figure 7f showing UMAP, and references a previous study.

claim: The expression of Spar peaks around zeitgeber time 10 (ZT10) (coinciding with the evening peak of locomotor activity).
source: Additionally, we noted that the expression of Spar peaks around zeitgeber time 10 (ZT10) (coinciding with the evening peak of locomotor activity) (Figure 7g and h), although the differences in expression level around the clock with LD or DD cycle were not dramatic (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 7g and 7h showing expression over time.

claim: A subset of Spar-positive larval CNS neurons are Clk856-Gal4>UAS GFP positive.
source: To confirm the expression of Spar in circadian neurons at the protein level, we co-stained Spar with a clock neuron reporter (Clk856-Gal4>UAS GFP). A subset of Spar-positive larval CNS neurons appeared to be Clk856-Gal4>UAS GFP positive (Figure 7i–j'').
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 7i-j'' showing co-labeling.

claim: A subset of Spar-positive neurons in adults are GFP-positive (Clk856-Gal4>UAS GFP), confirming the expression of Spar protein in LNv clock neurons.
source: Similarly, a subset of Spar-positive neurons in adults were GFP-positive (Figure 7k–l''), confirming the expression of Spar protein in LNv clock neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 7k-l'' showing co-labeling.

claim: Both AlkΔRA and SparΔExon1 mutant flies displayed a significantly reduced lifespan when compared to w1118 controls.
source: Both AlkΔRA and SparΔExon1 mutant flies displayed a significantly reduced lifespan when compared to w1118 controls, with the SparΔExon1 group exhibiting a significant reduction in survival at 25 days (Figure 8a).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8a showing survival curves.

claim: Both AlkΔRA and SparΔExon1 flies exhibited two major activity peaks, the first centered around ZT0, the beginning of the light phase, the so-called morning peak, and the second around ZT12, the beginning of the dark phase that is called the evening peak.
source: Activity analysis in AlkΔRA and SparΔExon1 flies under 12 hr light:12 hr dark (LD) conditions indicated that both AlkΔRA and SparΔExon1 flies exhibited two major activity peaks, the first centered around ZT0, the beginning of the light phase, the so-called morning peak, and the second around ZT12, the beginning of the dark phase that is called the evening peak (Figure 8b, black arrows).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8b showing activity profiles.

claim: SparΔExon1 flies exhibited increased activity, that was more prominent during the light phase, with an increase in the anticipatory activity preceding both the night-day and the day-night transition in comparison to AlkΔRA and w1118.
